transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I keep making these small mistakes in things that really should be straightforward. Like, I’ll turn in applications or research notes and then later notice something embarrassing — a mislabeled artwork date, or I skipped a question entirely — and the frustrating part is I honestly thought I had checked it.

It’s not like I’m trying to rush through everything carelessly, at least not on purpose. I’ll look over it and feel like, okay, this is done, this is fine, and then someone points out this tiny but obvious thing I missed. It’s been happening enough that I’m starting to worry it’s not just random. It feels kind of embarrassing, especially because these are the kinds of details I feel like I should be able to catch.
Do you find yourself checking your work over and over because you feel driven to make sure it’s exactly right?

I don’t think so, not in that exact way. I mean, I do check things, especially if I’m worried I might have missed something, but it doesn’t feel like I’m driven to keep checking until it’s perfect or like I can’t stop myself. It’s more like I’ll look it over, maybe even more than once, and then I assume I caught everything — and then later it turns out I didn’t.

So it’s not really this feeling of needing it to be exactly right in a perfectionistic way, I guess. It’s more frustrating because I think I checked it, but the checking somehow doesn’t actually catch the obvious mistake.
When you’re doing these tasks, do you often find your attention drifting even when you’re trying to focus?

Yeah, that happens a lot. I’ll be at my desk trying to read something or write notes, and I really do intend to stay with it, but my attention just kind of slips away.

It can be something outside, like a siren going by, or someone talking in the hallway, and then suddenly I’m listening to that instead of what’s in front of me. Or sometimes it’s not even anything external — I’ll have some random thought, like an idea for an exhibit or how something could be arranged, and I follow that in my head for a while. Then I sort of come back and realize I’ve been off-task for, I don’t know, twenty minutes or something, and the page is still sitting there barely changed.

It’s frustrating because it doesn’t feel like I’m choosing to stop focusing. It’s more like my brain just quietly wanders off, and I don’t notice right away.
Do you remember having these kinds of attention problems when you were a child?

Yeah, I think so. I didn’t really think of it that way at the time, obviously, but looking back it was kind of there even in elementary school.

I remember teachers would write things like, “has good ideas,” or that I understood the material, but then there’d always be this other part — like I forgot to turn in worksheets, or I’d lose the instruction sheet, or I’d miss some small detail that everyone else seemed to catch. It wasn’t usually that I didn’t know what to do. It was more like the paper disappeared into my backpack, or I did most of it but skipped one section without realizing, and then it became this whole thing.

My parents used to check my backpack almost every night for a while, because if they didn’t, there would be crumpled worksheets at the bottom or something I was supposed to bring back to school. I remember feeling embarrassed about it, because I wasn’t trying to be irresponsible. I’d just honestly think I had everything handled, and then someone would find something I missed.
Do these attention problems happen in other parts of your life too, like at home or in conversations with people?

Yeah, definitely. It’s not only with school or work-type stuff. It shows up at home and just in normal everyday responsibilities too.

Like, I’ll fully intend to return an email — not even an important dramatic one, just a normal “I should respond to that later today” kind of thing — and then somehow it’s three or four days later and I realize I never answered it at all. Same with bills sometimes. I’ll see the reminder or think, “Okay, I need to pay that,” and I don’t feel like I’m avoiding it exactly. It just kind of drops out of my mind once I’m not looking at it.

Groceries are another one. I’ll mean to pick something up, and even if it’s something basic, I can come home without it because I got distracted or I just forgot the specific thing I went for. Then I’m standing in the kitchen realizing, “Right, that was the whole reason I went.”

It’s embarrassing because these are normal adult things, and I feel like I should be able to just keep them in my head. But unless something is right in front of me or I’m reminded at the right moment, it can disappear on me.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about everyday things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?

I don’t think so, not a lot. I mean, I worry about normal things sometimes, like if I’ve forgotten something or if there’s something I’m supposed to deal with, but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting around constantly worrying when nothing is happening.

It’s more like, if there’s an actual reason in front of me, then sure, I can get concerned. But just ongoing everyday worry for no clear reason… I don’t really notice that as a big thing for me. At least not compared to the attention stuff we were talking about.
